Presence
prez'ens
n. (the state of being before or with; rendering Hebrew panim, Greek prosopon)
From the Latin praesentia, from praesum, to be before. The Hebrew word is panim, face — to be in God's presence is to be before his face, and to be banished is to be sent out from it, which is why the Hebrew idiom for exile and for judgment is the same idiom.

Biblical Definition

Presence in Scripture is not the doctrine of omnipresence but the covenant nearness of God to his people, and the whole Bible can be read as the story of its loss and recovery. Because the Hebrew word is face, presence is personal and relational rather than spatial. The first exile is described in exactly these terms: “And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod” (Genesis 4:16) — God is not absent from Nod, yet Cain has genuinely lost something. To Moses, hesitating at the prospect of leading a stiffnecked people, God gives the promise that settles everything: “My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest” (Exodus 33:14). David, after his great sin, asks not to keep his throne but to keep the face of God: “Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me” (Psalm 51:11). And the Psalter names what is finally there: “in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore” (Psalm 16:11). Hell in Scripture is destruction from the presence of the Lord; heaven is that presence unveiled. The tabernacle, the temple, the incarnation, the indwelling Spirit, and the new Jerusalem are the successive stages by which God brings his face back to men.

Webster 1828 Definition

The state of being before God's face. Hebrew panim is literally face, so presence is covenant nearness rather than bare omnipresence — heaven is that face unveiled, hell is banishment from it.

expand to see more

PRESENCE, n. prez'ens. [L. praesentia, from praesum, to be before.] The existence of a person or thing in a certain place; opposed to absence.

2. A being in company or in view; as, admitted to the presence of the king.

3. The person of a superior; approach face to face.

4. In theology, the presence of God, his special manifestation to his people, as distinguished from his omnipresence.

5. In Scripture, cast me not away from thy presence, Psa. 51; in thy presence is fulness of joy, Psa. 16.

Key Scripture

Genesis 4:16 — "And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod, on the east of Eden."

Exodus 33:14 — "And he said, My presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest."

Psalm 51:11 — "Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me."

Psalm 16:11 — "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore."

Modern Corruption

Presence has become a word for atmosphere — a mood produced in a room by music and lighting, spoken of as though it could be summoned. Scripture treats God's presence as a covenant gift, promised, withdrawn in judgment, and finally given in Christ.

expand to see more

Where a service is arranged to generate a felt sense of nearness and that sensation is then identified as the presence of God, two things go wrong at once. The regulative principle is set aside, since worship is now shaped by what produces the effect rather than by what God commanded; and the believer's assurance is tied to his feelings, so that a dry heart is read as a departed God. Exodus 33:14 gives the better ground: my presence shall go with thee is a promise, and promises are believed rather than felt.

The opposite error is nearer to the doctrinally careful. If presence is flattened into omnipresence — God is everywhere, therefore no more here than anywhere — then Genesis 4:16 and Psalm 51:11 become unintelligible, and so does the tabernacle. Scripture plainly means something by presence that it does not mean by omnipresence. The principle to recover is that God draws near covenantally to a particular people in a particular way, that this nearness was purchased at the cross by the One forsaken outside the camp, and that its final form is a city where his servants shall see his face.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew panim is face, and the idiom before the face of gives the whole vocabulary of presence and banishment. Greek prosopon is likewise face, and parousia is presence or arrival, the New Testament word for Christ's coming.

expand to see more

Hebrew panim (H6440) — face, presence; the plural form used of both God and men.

Hebrew lechem panim — bread of the face, rendered shewbread; loaves set continually before the LORD.

Hebrew shakan (H7931) — to dwell, to tabernacle; the root behind the later term shekinah.

Greek prosopon (G4383) — face, countenance, presence; used of seeing God face to face.

Greek parousia (G3952) — presence, arrival, coming; the standard term for the second advent.

Usage

"Of banishment as loss of the divine face: Cain went out from the presence of the LORD (Genesis 4:16)."

"Of the promise that settled Moses: my presence shall go with thee, and I will give thee rest (Exodus 33:14)."

"Of the final blessedness: in thy presence is fulness of joy (Psalm 16:11)."
